sweep_summary: Estonian (esto1258), catalog classification weight-hedged on Asu & Teras 2009 JIPA. Of the 11 works with stress in the title, 3 are not about Estonian (Wightman 1992, Turk 1992, Turk et al. 2006), 3 are sentence-prosody or quantity works (Sahkai & Tamm 2018/2019, Lehiste 2012), and 5 bear on word prosody: Eek 1990 (Linguistica Uralica, CC-BY, downloaded and read: foot-based account with main stress on the most prominent first foot, rhythmic secondary stress, morphemic suffix stress, no adjacent stresses - refines), Prince 1980 (LI, JSTOR-paywalled, no open copy - high priority, the metrical source behind the weight wording), Eek 1987 (De Gruyter paywalled, stress-perception experiment - medium), Eek et al. 1997 and Lehiste 1997 (Tallinn 1997 symposium volume, print-only per ESTER, ISBN 9985851471 - low/medium). Sahkai & Tamm 2019 was downloaded (Internet Archive copy of the CC-BY PDF) and is silent on word stress. Two authoritative first-hand Estonian-language statements already held by the project from the 9/16 download were read: Asu, Lippus, Pajusalu & Teras 2016 (EKH sec. 4.2, p. 127) confirms initial primary stress with rhythmic odd-syllable secondary stress subject to morphology; Eesti grammatika 2023 (FO 34-36, pp. 71-73) states the rule most explicitly, including the Q3 (overlong) condition for stress on the second syllable and secondary stress on heavy final syllables, and is proposed as the new deciding source (refines, consistent with weight-hedged). searches were done through Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, Europe PMC, Glottolog, ESTER and direct downloads.

new_statements.reading: Primary stress fixed on the initial syllable (lexical exceptions: interjections, recent loans, suffix -nna). Secondary stress is basically rhythmic, on odd-numbered syllables (syllabic trochees), but (i) an overlong (Q3) initial syllable licenses secondary stress on the immediately following syllable (ohtlik, armsalt, aastaid), (ii) a word-final syllable closed by a long plosive or a cluster takes secondary stress (raamatut, raamatust), and (iii) suffixes like -lik, -stik, -mine attract secondary stress inconsistently; final secondary stresses can be lost in spontaneous speech. This is exactly the 'weight-hedged' picture: initial primary stress, secondary stress rhythmic with weight (Q3 / heavy final) and morphological interference. Asu et al. 2016 (EKH, sec. 4.2 p. 127) says the same in slightly less detail, and Eek 1990 (LU 26: 258-259, downloaded open) gives the foot-based phonetic version with morphemic suffix stress and avoidance of adjacent stresses.

tone_statements.quote: Üldiselt on eesti keeles põhitoon langev. Kui esimeses ja teises vältes on põhitooni tipp rõhulise ja rõhutu silbi piiril, siis kolmandas vältes on see juba rõhulise silbi alguses. [...] Põhitoonikontuur tõepoolest on määrava tähtsusega teise ja kolmanda välte eristamisel. Selgub, et kui teise välte põhitoon (f0 langeb silbipiiril) panna kokku kolmanda välte silbisuhetega, siis ei tajuta seda sõna kolmandavältelisena. tone_statements.translation: In general F0 in Estonian is falling. Whereas in Q1 and Q2 the F0 peak is at the boundary of the stressed and unstressed syllable, in Q3 it is already at the beginning of the stressed syllable. [...] The F0 contour is indeed decisive in distinguishing Q2 from Q3. If a Q2 F0 contour (fall at the syllable boundary) is combined with Q3 syllable ratios, the word is not perceived as Q3; conversely, a Q3 F0 contour with Q2 syllable ratios is perceived as Q3. So changing only the pitch can change the meaning of a word.
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 contours (Q1/Q2 late fall vs Q3 early fall)

Ilse Lehiste (2003) on välja käinud arvamuse, et eesti keel on muutumas kvantiteedikeelest tooniaktsendikeeleks. [...] Nüüd tulebki mängu jalale iseloomulik põhitoonikontuur, mis III vältes on surutud kokku ühte silpi, I ja II vältes aga ulatub üle kahe silbi. tone_statements.translation: Several studies have shown that F0 really is important in distinguishing the 2nd and 3rd quantity (see the thorough overview in Lippus 2016: 140-148). Ilse Lehiste (2003) proposed that Estonian is changing from a quantity language into a tone-accent language. [...] Now the foot's characteristic F0 contour comes into play, which in Q3 is compressed into one syllable but in Q1 and Q2 extends over two syllables. A Q2 word could have the same prosodic structure as a Q3 word if the tonal contour stayed as it was. In that case Q2 and Q3 would be distinguished only by the location of the F0 fall in the word; there would no longer be a quantity contrast.

tone_statements.quote: Additionally the long and overlong quantity degrees are also marked by different pitch patterns. The thesis focuses on two main aspects: firstly, what is the role of the tonal component in Estonian quantity system, and secondly, how are the acoustic features of quantity realized in spontaneous Estonian? Both the perception tests and the acoustic study show the importance of the pitch in Estonian word prosody. If the phrase-level intonation is considered, pitch is a decisive factor between long and overlong quantities also in connected speech.

tone.translation: Several studies have shown that F0 really is important in distinguishing the 2nd and 3rd quantity (see the thorough overview in Lippus 2016: 140-148). Ilse Lehiste (2003) proposed that Estonian is changing from a quantity language into a tone-accent language. [...] Now the foot's characteristic F0 contour comes into play, which in Q3 is compressed into one syllable but in Q1 and Q2 extends over two syllables. A Q2 word could have the same prosodic structure as a Q3 word if the tonal contour stayed as it was. In that case Q2 and Q3 would be distinguished only by the location of the F0 fall in the word; there would no longer be a quantity contrast.
